title: Writing his first piece at eleven
summary: He writes 'Won't You Be My Little Sweet Household Queen', has it notated by the Biddles' Irish maid, and copyrighted.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Now, this is another dose of it. So you know I'm not going to take up dentistry. So I started in now to be exactly what I am. It took a long time to do that, because I watched Eubie for two years, until then I got a notion I wanted to write a piece. So -- and this was another advancement in my education -- I wrote, I had a little piece and I told my father about it and he told the maid, the maid that worked where he -- at 142 Walnut St. for the Biddles, was a Irish lady that was raised in a convent. So she said, "Your son's eleven years old and he wrote a piece?" Said, "Well, have him come up and hum it for me and I will take it down for him and then he can send it and have it copyrighted."
Well, the little piece was called, "Won't You Be My Little Sweet Household Queen". As corny as it sounds...

That was the name of the piece. Well, I went up there, and she actually took it down and then made a piano copy. Well, with a piano out or anything, now, this was something, really something new in my life, see. I didn't know anybody could do anything without the instrument. See, so when she did this, and I said, "What was that?", and she said it was a solfeggio. Well, I knew just as much then as I knew before, 'cause she could have said, "Spaghetti" it'd have been all the same to me. Solfeggio. Anyhow, so I was very curious to know what

this was all about. And we copyrighted the piece. And my father and this woman laughed about it and they said, 'Well, your son is going to be a Mozart one day.' See. So, I missed Mozart, but I did get to be a W.C. Handy, so.
Do you still remember the piece?
Do you still remember the piece?
(singing), 'Won't you be my sweet little household queen?' That's the way it ended up, see, as corny as it could be.
